analysis.title: DB CoTD: Different Ways to Skin Capex
key_insights: The AI trade split into spenders and earners on 30 October 2025, the day after Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft reported. Meta fell 11.3% (worst day in three years) after guiding 2026 capex 'notably larger'. Microsoft fell 2.9% despite strong cloud numbers. Alphabet rose 2.5% after its first $100bn quarter.
The basket of over 100 global AI-related stocks is up about 18% since 29 October 2025. The gain hides a sort between companies that pay for AI and companies that get paid for it.
Spenders have mostly stalled since 29 October 2025: Microsoft about -2%, Meta about -6%, Broadcom about -15%, Amazon about +9%, Nvidia about +3%.

Sellers of AI infrastructure have soared: SK hynix and Samsung are up over 100%, Marvell, Seagate and Western Digital are further ahead, and TSMC is up about 60%, the best performer of the trillion-dollar market-cap club.

Apple (about +27%) and Alphabet (about +24%) are the two mega-cap exceptions. Apple has not joined the data-centre capex race. Alphabet is both a spender and a demonstrable earner, with Cloud, Search and YouTube benefiting from Gemini and AI Mode.

Investors appear willing to fund very large AI budgets when there is visible evidence the spending is already producing revenue growth. Alphabet started from lower expectations than Microsoft and Meta.

Physical bottlenecks (memory, storage, chip packaging, optical networking, servers) are outperforming. Software is underperforming, with Adobe, Intuit, ServiceNow, Salesforce and Wix all in the red, as investors treat AI as more likely to displace software than to be sold by it.

The split runs through Asia: Taiwanese and Korean hardware names (MediaTek, ASE, SK hynix) are among the biggest outperformers, while India's IT services firms (Infosys, Wipro, HCL, Tata) sit almost entirely below the line.
Oracle, CoreWeave and Super Micro, the names most tied to debt- or contract-funded build-outs, are each down 40-60% since 29 October 2025.

Most of the basket's gain has come from the $100bn-$1trn market-cap tier rather than the largest companies, as was previously the case. The unscaled second chart still shows how large the mega-caps are.

Mega-cap capex is the revenue of almost every infrastructure winner on the chart. The AI trade probably cracks if mega-cap spending unexpectedly slows or if investors stop believing the spending earns an adequate return.

sector_views.sector: Semiconductors and AI hardware (memory, storage, packaging, optical, servers)
sector_views.rationale: Physical bottleneck names are the clear outperformers and receive the hyperscalers' capex as revenue.
Adobe, Intuit, ServiceNow, Salesforce and Wix are all in the red as investors treat AI as more likely to displace software than to be sold by it.
Infosys, Wipro, HCL and Tata sit almost entirely below the line in the chart of AI-related stocks.

earnings_insights: Alphabet posted its first $100bn quarter, reported the day before 30 October 2025, and the shares rose 2.5% the next day.
Microsoft's cloud numbers were strong at the late-October 2025 report, but the shares fell 2.9% the next day.
Meta guided 2026 capex 'notably larger' at the late-October 2025 report, and the shares fell 11.3% the next day.
risk_factors: A surprise slowdown in mega-cap AI capex would cut the revenue of nearly every infrastructure winner.
Investors may stop believing the spending earns an adequate return.
Debt- or contract-funded build-outs (Oracle, CoreWeave, Super Micro) have already fallen 40-60%.
AI may displace software companies rather than being sold by them.
charts_described: Chart of over a hundred global AI-related stocks plotted by market cap on a log scale against performance since 29 October 2025. Text says the basket is up about 18%, with infrastructure and hardware names above the line and software and Indian IT services names below it.
A second chart without log scaling shows the size of the mega-cap names relative to the rest of the basket.

tension_points.bull_case: Investors will fund very large AI budgets when there is visible evidence the spending is producing revenue growth, as with Alphabet's cloud and search products, and infrastructure suppliers keep receiving mega-cap capex as revenue.
tension_points.bear_case: Spenders such as Microsoft, Meta, Broadcom and Nvidia have gone nowhere, and leveraged builders (Oracle, CoreWeave, Super Micro) are down 40-60%, because investors doubt the return on the spending.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Mega-cap spending unexpectedly slows, or investors stop believing the spending generates an adequate return.

theme_stances.key_argument: The market now separates AI spenders from AI earners, and infrastructure suppliers have outperformed the companies writing the capex cheques.
theme_stances.evidence: the question is no longer whether AI will pay off, but for whom

theme_stances.key_argument: Outperformers are almost all physical bottlenecks in memory, storage, packaging, optical networking and servers, while software lags as investors judge AI more likely to eat software than be sold by it.
theme_stances.evidence: investors decide AI is more likely to eat software than be sold by it
